l: magic and enchantment, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Circe uses drugs, enchantments, and her wand to transform Ulysses's men into pigs and attempt to charm Ulysses. Moly prevents her drug from affecting Ulysses, while a second drug reverses the men's transformation.

l: Circe's transformation of the men, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Circe transforms the men who enter her house into pigs after giving them a drugged mixture and striking them with her wand. She later restores them by anointing each one with a second drug, making them human again, younger, taller, and better looking.

l: the voyage home, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Ulysses and his men are trying to continue their voyage home after reaching the Aeaean island. Circe tells them to remain with her until they regain their strength before resuming the journey.

l: death of Odysseus's comrades, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Ulysses and his men have already lost comrades before reaching the Aeaean island. The text says they are glad to have escaped death but does not give further details about those deaths in this unit.

l: Ulysses's sword, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Ulysses carries a bronze sword while reconnoitring and later takes it when he goes to Circe's house. Following Mercury's instructions, he draws it and rushes at Circe as though he intends to kill her.

l: Circe's wand, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Circe's wand is used to transform Ulysses's men into pigs and is raised when she attempts to transform Ulysses. She later carries it while opening the pigstye doors and restoring the men.

l: food and drink, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Ulysses and his men eat and drink their fill after killing the stag. Circe serves drugged cheese, honey, meal, and Pramnian wine to the men, while later providing abundant food and drink for the restored company.

l: Circe's oath, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Ulysses requires Circe to swear solemnly that she will plot no further harm against him before he will go to bed with her. Circe takes the oath, after which Ulysses trusts her enough to remain in her house and demand that she restore his men.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: Ulysses and his men stay with Circe for a whole year before deciding to resume their journey home. Circe tells Ulysses that they must first voyage to the house of Hades and Proserpine to consult the dead prophet Teiresias. She explains the route, the sacrifices required, and how Ulysses must protect Teiresias's access to the blood. As the men prepare to leave, Elpenor falls from the roof and dies, and Circe brings a ram and an ewe to the shore for the voyage.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: Ulysses agrees with his men that it is time to leave Circe and return home. He asks Circe to honor her promise to help him, learns that he must first consult Teiresias in Hades, and prepares his men for the journey.

l: Circe, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: Circe tells Ulysses that he must voyage to Hades and Proserpine's house before sailing home. She gives detailed instructions for reaching the place, offering sacrifices, and consulting Teiresias, then brings a ram and an ewe to the shore.

l: Ulysses's men, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: Ulysses's men remind him that they must think about returning home after a year with Circe. They are distressed when they learn that they must travel to Hades, but they follow Ulysses's orders and gather at the shore.

l: Teiresias, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: Teiresias is described as the blind Theban prophet whose reason remains unshaken after death. Ulysses must consult him because Proserpine has preserved his understanding, and Teiresias will explain the stages and course of Ulysses's voyage home.

l: Hades, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: Hades is the dark abode that Ulysses must visit before returning home. It lies near the meeting of Pyriphlegethon, Cocytus, and Acheron, and no ship can reach it directly as a port.

l: Proserpine, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: Proserpine's country lies beyond Oceanus, near groves of poplars and willows. Proserpine has left Teiresias his understanding after death, and Ulysses must go to her house to consult him.

l: ship, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: Circe tells Ulysses to raise the ship's mast and set its white sails so that the North Wind will carry it across Oceanus. The ship is to be beached on the shore of Proserpine's country before Ulysses proceeds to Hades.

l: ghosts of the dead, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: The dead ghosts are described as poor, feeble, and generally aimless after death, except for Teiresias. They will come to Ulysses when he offers the prescribed sacrifices, but he must keep them away from the blood until Teiresias has answered his questions.

l: stay with Circe, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: Ulysses and his men stay with Circe for a whole twelvemonth, feasting on large quantities of meat and wine. After the year has passed, they decide that it is time to leave and attempt to return home.

l: voyage to Hades, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: The voyage to Hades is required before Ulysses and his men can sail home. Circe directs them across Oceanus and instructs Ulysses to dig a trench, make offerings, pray to the dead, and seek Teiresias's guidance.

l: consultation with Teiresias, The Odyssey, “Thus did she speak and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole
s: The consultation with Teiresias is intended to reveal which stages Ulysses must make and how he should sail to reach his home. Ulysses must offer sacrifices and guard the blood so that Teiresias can answer his questions.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Ulysses sails with his companions to Oceanus and performs a necromantic sacrifice so that he can question the dead. Elpenor asks to be buried, while Teiresias warns Ulysses about Neptune, the Thrinacian island, the suitors in Ithaca, and his eventual death. Ulysses then speaks with his mother Anticlea, who tells him that Penelope remains faithful, Telemachus holds the estate, and his father suffers in the countryside. He also sees many famous women among the ghosts before deciding to leave the underworld.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Ulysses travels to the land of the Cimmerians to consult Teiresias. He performs sacrifices to summon the dead, speaks with Elpenor, Teiresias, Anticlea, and other ghosts, and learns about his difficult return to Ithaca.

l: Circe, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Circe sends Ulysses and his companions a steady fair wind toward Oceanus. She had instructed Ulysses about the place where he should perform the sacrifice.

l: Oceanus, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Oceanus is the deep river whose waters surround the land and city of the Cimmerians. Ulysses reaches its waters by ship and follows them to the place where he summons the dead.

l: Elpenor, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Elpenor appears as the first ghost because his body was left unwaked and unburied at Circe’s house. He explains that he fell from the roof while drunk and asks Ulysses to burn him, build a barrow by the sea, and plant his rowing oar over the grave.

l: ghosts of the dead, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: The ghosts come from Erebus after Ulysses pours blood into the trench. They include brides, bachelors, old men, maids, and warriors, but they cannot speak reasonably until they have tasted the blood.

l: Hades, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Hades is described as the gloomy house of the dead. Elpenor asks Ulysses to perform burial rites so that he will not remain improperly buried in Hades.

l: Anticlea, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Anticlea, Ulysses’s mother, appears among the dead and speaks with him after drinking the sacrificial blood. She says that Penelope remains in Ulysses’s house, Telemachus holds the estate, and Ulysses’s father lives miserably in the country; she says that longing for Ulysses and affection for him caused her death.

l: Teiresias, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Teiresias comes with a golden sceptre and drinks the blood before answering Ulysses’s questions. He prophesies Ulysses’s suffering, the danger posed by Neptune, the need to spare the Sun’s flocks, the slaughter of the suitors, a later journey with an oar, and a peaceful death in old age.

l: Neptune, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Neptune continues to resent Ulysses for blinding his son. Teiresias warns that Neptune will make Ulysses’s return difficult and later instructs Ulysses to sacrifice to Neptune in a land where people do not know the sea.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Ithaca is Ulysses’s homeland, which he has not yet reached after leaving for Troy. Teiresias says Ulysses may eventually return there, though he will arrive after great suffering and the loss of his men.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Telemachus remains in possession of Ulysses’s lands and must entertain people because of his position as a magistrate. Elpenor invokes him when asking Ulysses to fulfill the rites for his burial.

l: Penelope, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Penelope remains in Ulysses’s house and spends her days and nights grieving for him. Teiresias says that suitors are pressing her while consuming Ulysses’s property under the pretext of courtship and gifts.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: The suitors overrun Ulysses’s house and consume his possessions while courting Penelope. Teiresias says that Ulysses will kill them by force or fraud after returning home.

l: the underworld visit, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: The underworld visit takes Ulysses to the Cimmerians’ land beyond Oceanus. During the visit he summons the dead, receives Teiresias’s prophecy, speaks with Anticlea, and sees the ghosts of famous women.

l: necromantic sacrifice, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Ulysses digs a trench, pours offerings of honey and milk, wine, and water, scatters barley meal, and sacrifices two sheep. Their blood draws the ghosts near, but Ulysses prevents them from drinking until Teiresias has answered him.

l: the prophecy of Teiresias, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Teiresias’s prophecy says that Ulysses will suffer on his return because of Neptune, must restrain his companions and spare the Sun’s flocks, and will otherwise lose his ship and men. It also foretells the suitors’ slaughter, a journey carrying an oar into an inland country, sacrifices to Neptune, and a gentle death in old age.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Ulysses’s return to Ithaca will be difficult and will follow the loss of his companions if the Sun’s flocks are harmed. He will find trouble in his house, kill the suitors, and later undertake the journey with the oar described by Teiresias.

l: Thrinacian island, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: The Thrinacian island contains the sheep and cattle belonging to the Sun. Teiresias warns Ulysses to leave these flocks unharmed, since harming them will bring destruction to his ship and men.

l: oar (Elpenor's oar), The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Elpenor asks Ulysses to place the oar he used while alive over his grave as a memorial. Teiresias separately commands Ulysses to carry a well-made oar inland until someone mistakes it for a winnowing shovel.

l: revenge upon the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Teiresias foretells that Ulysses will take revenge on the suitors after returning home. Ulysses will kill them in his own house, using force or fraud.

l: death, The Odyssey, BOOK XI
s: Teiresias says that Ulysses’s death will come from the sea when he is full of years and peace of mind. His life will ebb away gently, and his people will bless him.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Ulysses finishes recounting his underworld journey to the Phaeacians, describing the dead he encountered after visiting Hades. Agamemnon son of Atreus tells Ulysses that Aegisthus and Clytemnestra murdered him after welcoming him home from Troy. Achilles asks about his son Neoptolemus and father Peleus, while Ajax refuses to speak to Ulysses because of their dispute over Achilles’ armor. Ulysses also describes seeing Minos, Orion, Tityus, Tantalus, Sisyphus, and the phantom of Hercules before fleeing Hades and returning to his ship.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Ulysses agrees to continue telling his story at Alcinous’s request and recounts his encounters with the dead during his underworld journey. He speaks with Agamemnon, Achilles, and other ghosts, attempts to reconcile with Ajax, and finally flees Hades after fearing that Proserpine might send up the Gorgon.

l: Phaeacians, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: The Phaeacians listen enthralled and speechless as Ulysses finishes his account. They are urged by Arete and Alcinous to honor him with gifts and an escort home.

l: Alcinous, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Alcinous praises Ulysses’s language and asks him to continue describing the heroes who went to Troy and died. He promises that the Phaeacians will provide Ulysses with gifts and an escort.

l: Agamemnon, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Agamemnon son of Atreus tells Ulysses that Aegisthus and Clytemnestra murdered him after Aegisthus feasted him in his house. He warns Ulysses not to trust women completely or reveal all his plans to his wife, though he praises Penelope and asks whether his son Orestes is alive.

l: Aegisthus, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Aegisthus welcomes Agamemnon to his house, feasts him, and then massacres him and his companions.

l: Clytemnestra, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Clytemnestra helps murder Agamemnon and kills Cassandra beside him. Agamemnon condemns her as cruel and shameless for murdering her husband and denying him the comfort of seeing his son.

l: Achilles, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Achilles’s ghost meets Ulysses in Hades and says that he would rather be a living servant than rule among the dead. He asks about Neoptolemus and Peleus, and is pleased when Ulysses praises Neoptolemus’s courage and conduct at Troy.

l: Troy, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Troy is the place where Achilles’s son Neoptolemus fights bravely, kills Eurypylus and many others, enters the horse made by Epeus, and receives his share of the spoils after the city is sacked.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Ithaca is Ulysses’s intended home, though he has not yet been able to reach it or set foot in his own country. Agamemnon advises him to approach it secretly and not announce the arrival of his ship.

l: Hades, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Hades is the realm where Ulysses encounters the ghosts of the dead. It contains the dead gathered around Minos, the punished figures of Tityus, Tantalus, and Sisyphus, and the phantom of Hercules.

l: the underworld visit, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: During his underworld journey, Ulysses consults the dead and hears their accounts of death, grief, punishment, and heroic fame. He ends the journey by returning to his ship on the river Oceanus after becoming frightened by the multitude of ghosts.

l: ghosts of the dead, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: The ghosts of the dead gather around Ulysses and tell him their melancholy stories. They include Agamemnon, Achilles, Ajax, Minos, Orion, Tityus, Tantalus, Sisyphus, and the phantom of Hercules.

l: women’s betrayal, The Odyssey, Here he ended, and the guests sat all of them enthralled and speechless
s: Women’s betrayal is associated with the deaths of Agamemnon and his companions through the actions of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus. Agamemnon warns Ulysses to be cautious with women, while distinguishing Penelope as admirable and trustworthy.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Circe tells Ulysses and his crew about the dangers ahead on their journey home. She warns them about the Sirens, the Wanderers, Scylla, and Charybdis, explaining how to pass each danger. She also warns them not to harm the cattle and sheep of the sun-god on the Thrinacian island. Ulysses and his crew have returned from the house of Hades after burying Elpenor on the Aeaean island.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Ulysses returns with his crew from the house of Hades and listens to Circe's instructions about the dangers ahead. He asks whether there is any way to escape Charybdis while also protecting his men from Scylla.

l: Ulysses's men, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Odysseus's crew returns from the house of Hades and helps bury Elpenor. They are instructed to stop their ears with wax near the Sirens, bind Ulysses to the mast if he wishes to hear the Sirens' song, and drive the ship quickly between Scylla and Charybdis.

l: ship, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: The ship is drawn onto the sands of the Aeaean island after crossing the river Oceanus. Circe warns that the ship and its crew will be destroyed if the cattle and sheep of the sun-god are harmed.

l: Circe, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Circe welcomes Ulysses and his crew after their return from the house of Hades, provides them with food and wine, and explains their future course. She warns them about the Sirens, the Wanderers, Scylla, Charybdis, and the cattle and sheep of the sun-god.

l: house of Hades, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Ulysses and his crew have returned alive from the house of Hades. Circe says that going there alive means they will have died twice while others have died once.

l: the Sirens, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: The Sirens sit in a green field and enchant those who come near them. Their victims never return to their wives and children, and a heap of dead men's bones lies around them with flesh rotting from it.

l: the Sirens' song, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: The Sirens' song is so sweet that it warbles those who hear it to death. Ulysses may listen if his crew stop their ears and bind him upright to the mast, tightening his bonds if he begs to be released.

l: Wanderers, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: The Wanderers are overhanging rocks struck by the deep blue waves of Amphitrite. No bird may pass them safely, and no ship except the Argo has ever sailed through them and escaped.

l: Scylla, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Scylla is an invincible, savage monster with twelve feet, six long necks, and six heads bearing three rows of teeth each. She lives in a cavern and catches sea creatures and men, taking one man in each mouth when a ship passes.

l: Scylla's rock, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Scylla's rock rises sheer toward heaven and has a peak hidden in a dark cloud. A high cavern in its side faces west and is the place where Scylla sits.

l: Charybdis, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Charybdis lies beneath a large fig tree on the lower rock opposite Scylla. She vomits out the waters three times a day and sucks them down three times a day, and any ship caught in her sucking cannot be saved even by Neptune.

l: Thrinacian island, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: The Thrinacian island contains seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep belonging to the sun-god, with fifty animals in each group. The animals do not breed or diminish and are tended by Phaethusa and Lampetie.

l: the sun-god Hyperion, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: The sun-god owns the cattle and sheep on the Thrinacian island. Circe warns that anyone who harms them will bring destruction on the ship and comrades.

l: Sun-god Hyperion, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Hyperion is identified as the sun-god and as the father of Phaethusa and Lampetie by Neaera.

l: the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: The cattle of the sun-god are kept on the Thrinacian island in seven herds of fifty head each. They neither breed nor become fewer, and Circe warns Ulysses's crew to leave them unharmed.

l: the sheep of the sun-god, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: The sheep of the sun-god are kept on the Thrinacian island in seven flocks of fifty each. They neither breed nor become fewer, and harming them is forbidden.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Ithaca is the home that Ulysses may still reach after much hardship if the cattle and sheep of the sun-god are left unharmed.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Circe explains the dangers that Ulysses and his crew must face during their journey home. If they leave the sun-god's herds and flocks unharmed, they may reach Ithaca after much hardship.

l: passage between Scylla and Charybdis, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Circe instructs Ulysses to hug the side of Scylla and drive the ship past quickly. She says it is better to lose six men to Scylla than to lose the entire crew to Charybdis.

l: destruction of the ship and comrades, The Odyssey, BOOK XII
s: Circe warns that harming the cattle or sheep of the sun-god will cause the destruction of the ship and Ulysses's comrades. Even if Ulysses himself escapes, he will return late and in poor condition after losing all his men.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Ulysses and his men sail past the Sirens and through the Straits of Scylla and Charybdis, where Scylla seizes six men. They land on the island of the sun-god Hyperion despite warnings, and after their provisions run out, Eurylochus persuades the men to slaughter the sun-god's cattle. Jove destroys their ship with lightning, killing all the men except Ulysses. Ulysses survives on a makeshift raft and is eventually carried to the Ogygian island, where Calypso receives him.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Ulysses tells his men Circe's prophecies and orders them to bind him to the mast so that he can hear the Sirens without steering the ship toward them. He leads the men through the Straits of Scylla and Charybdis, but does not tell them about Scylla because he fears they would stop rowing. After the shipwreck, he survives on the mast and keel, escapes Charybdis, and is carried to the Ogygian island.

l: Ulysses's men, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Ulysses's men bind him to the mast, plug their own ears with wax, and row past the Sirens. They later land on the island of the sun-god, break their oath by slaughtering the cattle, and are all killed when Jove destroys their ship.

l: Eurylochus, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Eurylochus gives an insolent answer when Ulysses tells the men to avoid the island of the sun-god. He later gives the men the evil counsel to kill the sun-god's cattle, arguing that death by lightning would be preferable to starvation.

l: Circe, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Circe befriends Ulysses's crew with a favorable wind and warns Ulysses about the Sirens, Scylla, Charybdis, and the island of the sun-god. She tells him that the island will bring the crew's worst danger and instructs him to avoid it.

l: the Sirens, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The Sirens sit in a field of flowers on their island and sing to passing sailors. They sing to Ulysses and promise that their song will charm him and make him wiser by revealing what happened before Troy and what will happen throughout the world.

l: Scylla, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Scylla lives on one side of the dangerous straits and suddenly seizes six of Ulysses's best men. She carries them to her rock, where she munches them at the mouth of her den.

l: Charybdis, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Charybdis lies opposite Scylla and repeatedly sucks down and vomits up the salt water, creating a deafening whirlpool. After the shipwreck, she draws Ulysses's raft toward her, but Ulysses escapes by clinging to a fig tree and later returning to the raft.

l: ship, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The ship carries Ulysses and his men past the Sirens, through the straits, and to the island of the sun-god. After the men slaughter the cattle, Jove's thunderbolts break the ship apart, killing the crew and leaving Ulysses with only its mast and keel.

l: the Straits of Scylla and Charybdis, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The Straits contain Scylla on one side and Charybdis on the other. Ulysses's ship passes through them in terror, losing six men to Scylla while avoiding the whirlpool.

l: Thrinacian island, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The island contains the sun-god's cattle and sheep. Ulysses warns his men to avoid it, but they land there because they are exhausted and later remain for a month while unfavorable winds prevent their departure.

l: the Ogygian island, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The Ogygian island is where the gods eventually strand Ulysses after his raft carries him for nine days. The powerful goddess Calypso dwells there and takes Ulysses in.

l: the sun-god Hyperion, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The sun-god Hyperion owns the cattle and sheep on the island. He becomes enraged when Ulysses's men kill his cattle and asks Jove to punish them.

l: the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The cattle of the sun-god are described as fair and goodly and are guarded as the property of Hyperion. Ulysses's men slaughter the best of them after their provisions run out, and supernatural signs follow, including hides that crawl and meat that lows like cattle.

l: Jove, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Jove agrees to punish Ulysses's crew for killing the sun-god's cattle. After the ship leaves the island, he raises a storm and destroys the ship with thunderbolts, killing the men.

l: Calypso, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Calypso tells Ulysses about Jove's promise to punish the crew, saying that she learned it from Mercury. She dwells on the Ogygian island and receives Ulysses kindly after he is stranded there.

l: immortal gods, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The gods send a favorable wind for Ulysses's voyage but also bring dangers and punishments upon the crew. They send signs after the cattle are slaughtered, and they strand Ulysses on the Ogygian island after the shipwreck.

l: the Sirens' song, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The Sirens' song is exceptionally beautiful and promises knowledge of the past and future. Ulysses longs to hear more of it, but his men row faster and bind him more tightly until the ship is out of hearing.

l: Circe's prophecies, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Circe's prophecies warn Ulysses to avoid the Sirens, pass between Scylla and Charybdis, and keep away from the island of the sun-god. Ulysses shares these warnings with his men, though he withholds the danger posed by Scylla.

l: the oath not to kill the sun-god's cattle, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Ulysses makes his men swear that they will not kill any cattle or sheep on the sun-god's island. The men repeat the promise, but later violate it after their food supplies are exhausted.

l: the slaughter of the sun-god's cattle, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: Eurylochus persuades the starving men to slaughter the best of the sun-god's cattle as a sacrifice. They feast on the cattle for six days, provoking the sun-god's anger and the punishment that follows.

l: the shipwreck, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: After the crew leaves the island of the sun-god, Jove sends a storm that snaps the mast and fills the ship with fire and brimstone. The ship is destroyed, the helmsman and all the other men die, and Ulysses survives by fastening the mast to the keel.

l: the voyage home, The Odyssey, “Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,
s: The voyage home is interrupted by the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, the island of the sun-god, and the shipwreck. Ulysses alone continues after the wreck and is eventually carried to the Ogygian island.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Ulysses is carried from Scheria to Ithaca by the Phaeacians, who leave him sleeping with his gifts in the harbour of Phorcys. Neptune transforms the returning Phaeacian ship into stone and threatens the Phaeacians with further punishment. Minerva reveals Ithaca to Ulysses, helps him hide his treasure in the Cave of the Naiads, and urges him to conceal his return while preparing revenge upon the suitors. She disguises Ulysses as an old beggar and sends him to the swineherd, while she goes to Sparta to see his son.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Ulysses leaves Scheria with gifts, is carried asleep to Ithaca, and initially fails to recognize his homeland because of the mist. He lies to Minerva about his identity and circumstances until she reveals herself, then hides his treasure with her and agrees to disguise himself while planning against the suitors.

l: Alcinous, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Alcinous arranges for the Phaeacians to give Ulysses additional tripods and cauldrons and ensures that his gifts are securely stowed. He sends Ulysses to his ship and later recognizes Neptune’s punishment of the Phaeacians as the fulfillment of an old prophecy.

l: Phaeacians, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: The Phaeacians give Ulysses valuable gifts and carry him safely from Scheria to Ithaca while he sleeps. Neptune transforms their returning ship into stone, and they fear that he will also bury their city under a mountain.

l: Neptune, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Neptune remains angry because the Phaeacians have escorted Ulysses safely home and loaded him with gifts. With Jove’s approval, he turns the returning Phaeacian ship into stone and drives it into the ground near Scheria.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Minerva causes mist to conceal Ithaca and Ulysses’ arrival, then appears first as a shepherd and later reveals herself. She helps him hide his treasure, explains the situation at his house, disguises him as an old and unattractive man, and goes to Sparta to see his son.

l: Penelope, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Penelope remains at home grieving for Ulysses and has no peace because of her constant tears. The suitors court her, while she gives them messages that encourage them but means the opposite of what she says.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Telemachus is Ulysses’ son and is staying with Menelaus at Lacedaemon. Minerva goes to Sparta to see him while Ulysses begins his concealed return.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: The suitors have been ruling in Ulysses’ house for three years and consuming his substance while courting Penelope. Minerva and Ulysses plan their destruction, and she intends to conceal Ulysses from them until he is ready to act.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Ithaca is Ulysses’ rugged island homeland, known for its corn, wine, cattle, goats, timber, and unfailing watering places. Ulysses reaches it by ship but does not recognize it until Minerva disperses the mist.

l: Scheria, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Scheria is the home of the Phaeacians, who escort Ulysses to Ithaca and provide him with gifts. Neptune later turns the returning ship to stone near Scheria and threatens the city with burial under a mountain.

l: Ithacan harbor of Phorcys, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: The harbour of the old merman Phorcys lies between two points that shelter it from storms. It contains the olive tree and the Cave of the Naiads, and the Phaeacians land Ulysses there while he is asleep.

l: Cave of the Naiads, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: The Cave of the Naiads is a sacred cavern near the harbour of Phorcys, with stone mixing bowls, wine-jars, water, and looms on which the nymphs weave sea-purple robes. Minerva and Ulysses use it to hide his gold, bronze, and clothing, sealing the entrance with a stone.

l: Phaeacian ship, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: The Phaeacian ship carries Ulysses swiftly from Scheria to Ithaca while he sleeps and runs partway onto the shore at the harbour of Phorcys. On its return journey, Neptune transforms it into stone and roots it in the ground.

l: Ulysses’ treasure, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Ulysses’ treasure consists of bronze, gold, clothing, tripods, cauldrons, and other gifts from the Phaeacians. He counts it after waking and finds nothing missing, then stores it with Minerva in the Cave of the Naiads.

l: Neptune’s transformation of the ship, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Neptune’s transformation turns the returning Phaeacian ship into stone and drives it into the ground near Scheria. The Phaeacians see that the ship has been rooted in the sea but do not understand what happened until they connect it with an old prophecy.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Ulysses returns to Ithaca asleep on a Phaeacian ship and is set down near the harbour of Phorcys with his gifts. Minerva conceals his arrival with mist, confirms that he is home, and directs him to remain unknown while he prepares to confront the suitors.

l: Ulysses's disguise, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Minerva disguises Ulysses by covering him with wrinkles, removing the appearance of his yellow hair, clothing him in a repulsive garment, and making his eyes bleary. The disguise is intended to prevent the suitors, Penelope, and his son from recognizing him.

l: revenge upon the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: Ulysses and Minerva consult about destroying the suitors, who have occupied his house and consumed his substance. Minerva promises to support him and begins by concealing his identity so that he can gather information before taking revenge.

l: Odyssey homeward voyage, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: The homeward voyage ends when the Phaeacians carry Ulysses from Scheria to Ithaca in a single night while he sleeps. After landing, the Phaeacians return home, while Neptune punishes their ship for assisting him.

l: Eumaeus, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: The swineherd is in charge of Ulysses’ pigs and is described as well affected toward Ulysses and devoted to Penelope and his son. Minerva directs the disguised Ulysses to stay with him near the rock called Raven by the fountain Arethusa.

l: the suitors’ courtship of Penelope, The Odyssey, BOOK XIII
s: The suitors have courted Penelope for three years and have offered wedding presents while ruling in Ulysses’ house. Penelope sends them encouraging messages while secretly meaning the opposite, and Minerva identifies their conduct as a reason for Ulysses’ planned revenge.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, “But why,” said Ulysses, “did you not tell him, for you knew all about
s: Ulysses asks Minerva why she did not tell Telemachus everything, since Telemachus might otherwise suffer hardship while others consume Ulysses's estate. Minerva says Telemachus is staying comfortably with Menelaus, while the suitors lie in wait at sea to kill him before he returns. She predicts that the suitors may die before they succeed. Minerva then disguises Ulysses as an aged, poor wanderer, and the two part, with Minerva going to Lacedaemon to fetch Telemachus.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, “But why,” said Ulysses, “did you not tell him, for you knew all about
s: Ulysses asks Minerva why she did not tell Telemachus what she knew. Minerva transforms him into an aged, ragged wanderer with wrinkles, bleared eyes, little hair, filthy clothes, a deer-skin garment, a staff, and a holed wallet.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, “But why,” said Ulysses, “did you not tell him, for you knew all about
s: Minerva tells Ulysses that Telemachus is staying comfortably with Menelaus and that the suitors are waiting to kill him. She transforms Ulysses into a poor old wanderer, then parts from him and goes to Lacedaemon to fetch Telemachus.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, “But why,” said Ulysses, “did you not tell him, for you knew all about
s: Telemachus is staying quite comfortably with Menelaus and has abundance of every kind. Minerva says she sent him so that he would be well spoken of for having gone.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, “But why,” said Ulysses, “did you not tell him, for you knew all about
s: The suitors have put out to sea and are lying in wait for Telemachus, intending to kill him before he can get home. Minerva thinks some of them may find graves before they succeed.

l: the estate of Ulysses, The Odyssey, “But why,” said Ulysses, “did you not tell him, for you knew all about
s: Ulysses's estate is being eaten up by the suitors while Telemachus is away.

l: Lacedaemon, The Odyssey, “But why,” said Ulysses, “did you not tell him, for you knew all about
s: Minerva goes straight to Lacedaemon to fetch Telemachus.

l: the suitors' plot to kill Telemachus, The Odyssey, “But why,” said Ulysses, “did you not tell him, for you knew all about
s: The suitors' plot is to wait at sea and kill Telemachus before he can return home. Minerva doubts that they will succeed.

l: Minerva's transformation of Ulysses, The Odyssey, “But why,” said Ulysses, “did you not tell him, for you knew all about
s: Minerva touches Ulysses with her wand and makes him look old and impoverished. She gives him wrinkles, bleared eyes, little hair, withered flesh, filthy tattered clothing, a deer-skin outer garment, a staff, and a holed wallet.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Ulysses reaches Eumaeus’s hut in Ithaca, where the swineherd protects him from the dogs and welcomes him with food and drink. Eumaeus explains his loyalty to Ulysses, the wealth of Ulysses’s estate, and the suitors’ abuse of it. Ulysses promises that he will return before the end of the year and take vengeance on the suitors, but Eumaeus does not believe him. Eumaeus also worries about Penelope, Laertes, and Telemachus, while Ulysses prepares to tell the story of his sufferings.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Ulysses travels to Eumaeus’s hut and is attacked by the hounds before Eumaeus drives them away. He eats and drinks while listening to Eumaeus, then claims that Ulysses will return within the year and take vengeance on those mistreating Penelope and Telemachus. He does not reveal his identity and offers to tell Eumaeus the story of his sufferings.

l: Eumaeus, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Eumaeus is described as Ulysses’s most thrifty servant and as a loyal swineherd who deeply mourns his master. He welcomes the disguised Ulysses, gives him food and drink, and explains the condition of Ulysses’s household. He believes that Ulysses is dead but wishes that he could return, and he worries about Telemachus’s safety.

l: Penelope, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Penelope is said to receive travelers who claim to have news of Ulysses, questioning them and grieving as they tell their stories. Eumaeus says that she hopes for Ulysses’s return and is suffering because the suitors are consuming his estate.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Telemachus has gone to Pylos to seek news of his father. The suitors are waiting for him on his return, hoping to destroy the house of Arceisius in Ithaca, and Eumaeus is anxious about his safety.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: The suitors consume the best pigs and other provisions from Ulysses’s estate without shame. They sacrifice animals, drink his wine, and force his servants to supply them, while waiting to attack Telemachus and marry Penelope.

l: pigs, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Eumaeus keeps hundreds of pigs in twelve styes and has additional boars outside the yards. The suitors continually eat the best boars, so Eumaeus must keep sending them the finest animals. Eumaeus sacrifices two young pigs to feed Ulysses.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Ithaca is the island where Ulysses’s household and Eumaeus’s pig yards are located. Travelers arrive there claiming to bring news of Ulysses, while the suitors consume his wealth and threaten his household.

l: the swineherd's hut, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Eumaeus’s hut stands beside the pig yards on a site visible from far away. He gives Ulysses a thick bed of rushes covered with a shaggy chamois skin and welcomes him inside for food and conversation.

l: the estate of Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Ulysses’s estate is described as exceptionally wealthy, including herds of cattle, flocks of sheep, droves of pigs, and large flocks of goats. The suitors waste this wealth by taking its animals, wine, and other provisions without restraint.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Ulysses declares that he will return within the same year, at the end of one moon and the beginning of the next. Eumaeus does not believe this prediction, though he wishes that Ulysses could come home.

l: revenge upon the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Ulysses says that, after returning, he will take vengeance on all those who mistreat Penelope and Telemachus. The suitors are the people he specifically threatens with this vengeance.

l: Ulysses's presumed death, The Odyssey, BOOK XIV
s: Eumaeus believes that Ulysses has been dead and gone for a long time. He says that wolves, birds of prey, or fish may have destroyed him and that his bones may lie buried on a foreign shore, although he continues to honor and grieve for him.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Ulysses, disguised as a Cretan stranger, tells Eumaeus a false account of his birth, warfare, travels, shipwreck, and alleged news of Ulysses. He claims that Jove caused his force to be defeated in Egypt, that he was later betrayed and nearly sold into slavery, and that he escaped to Ithaca. Eumaeus does not believe the story about Ulysses but offers hospitality out of respect for Jove. Eumaeus sacrifices a pig, shares supper with the stranger and the swineherds, gives him shelter, and then goes out to guard the pigs during the storm.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Ulysses disguises himself as an old Cretan stranger and tells Eumaeus an elaborate story about his birth, warfare, travels, shipwreck, and alleged knowledge of Ulysses. He remains unrecognized, receives food and shelter from Eumaeus, and sleeps in the swineherd's hut.

l: Eumaeus, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Eumaeus listens skeptically to the stranger's story and rejects his claim that Ulysses is about to return. Nevertheless, he treats the stranger kindly out of respect for Jove and hospitality, sacrifices a pig, shares supper, gives him a bed and a cloak, and guards the pigs through the storm.

l: Jove, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Jove is said to have caused the terrible expedition to Troy and to have devised misfortune for the disguised Ulysses. He sends panic during the Egyptian defeat, destroys the Phoenician ship with thunderbolts, protects strangers, and is invoked as a witness and in prayers.

l: Crete, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Crete is presented as the birthplace of the disguised stranger and the home of his father Castor son of Hylax. The stranger claims to have commanded Cretan men and ships and to have sailed from Crete on the raid against Egypt.

l: Egypt, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Egypt is the destination of the stranger's raid after the Trojan war. He claims that his men ravaged its land, were defeated, and that he remained among the Egyptians for seven years.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Ithaca is where the disguised Ulysses comes ashore after escaping from the ship that was allegedly taking him toward slavery. He hides near a wood and is then brought to a good man's door, Eumaeus's hut.

l: Troy, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Troy is the place where the Achaeans fought for nine years before sacking the city in the tenth year. The disguised Ulysses also recalls serving in an ambush near its walls.

l: Egyptian people, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The Egyptian people respond to the alarm caused by the raid by coming out with horsemen and foot soldiers. They kill many of Ulysses's men, capture the rest, and later give the disguised Ulysses gifts during his seven years among them.

l: immortal gods, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The immortal gods are credited with granting and withholding fortune. Eumaeus sacrifices to them and prays that Ulysses may return home.

l: Ulysses’s crew, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Ulysses's crew participates in the raid on Egypt, disobeys his orders, and ravages the land. Many are killed or captured by the Egyptians, while those aboard the Phoenician ship later perish in the storm.

l: swineherd’s men, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The swineherds bring the pigs into their styes, help prepare the five-year-old boar, and eat supper with Eumaeus and the disguised Ulysses. They sleep near the hut while Eumaeus goes out to guard the pigs.

l: Ulysses’s ships, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Before the Trojan expedition, Ulysses claims to have commanded men and ships on nine foreign campaigns. He later says that nine ships sailed from Crete toward Egypt, and that one Phoenician ship was destroyed by Jove after taking him aboard.

l: fleet (Ulysses’s fleet), The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The fleet of nine ships leaves Crete after six days of feasting and reaches the river Aegyptus on the fifth day. Ulysses stations the ships in the river while sending scouts inland.

l: cloak, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The disguised Ulysses uses a story about an ambush at Troy to prompt someone to give him a cloak. Eumaeus refuses to provide one for the next day but covers him with a heavy cloak kept for bad weather.

l: pigs, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The pigs are driven into their styes at night, and Eumaeus considers feeding the stranger from the labor of raising them. Eumaeus later leaves the hut to sleep near and protect them from possible attacks.

l: the Trojan War, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The Trojan expedition is said to have been demanded by the people of Crete, who required the disguised Ulysses and Idomeneus to lead their ships. It lasts nine years of fighting before the city is taken in the tenth.

l: sack of Troy, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The sack of Troy occurs in the tenth year of the war, after which the Achaeans sail home as heaven disperses them. The disguised Ulysses claims to spend only one month happily at home before planning the raid on Egypt.

l: the attack on Egypt, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The disguised Ulysses organizes a raid on Egypt after returning from Troy, equipping nine ships and gathering crews. His men disobey orders, leave the ships, and ravage the Egyptian land.

l: Egyptian defeat of Ulysses’s force, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The Egyptians surround Ulysses's force after the raid, and Jove spreads panic among the attackers. Many of Ulysses's men are killed and the survivors are captured for forced labor, while Ulysses saves himself by clasping the Egyptian king's knees.

l: the shipwreck, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: After the disguised Ulysses is placed on a ship bound for Libya, Jove raises a storm and destroys it with thunderbolts. The crew falls into the sea, while Ulysses survives by clinging to the mast.

l: Ulysses’s drifting at sea, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Ulysses claims to drift for nine days after the shipwreck, until a great wave carries him to the Thesprotian coast on the tenth night. Pheidon's son finds him nearly dead from cold and fatigue and brings him to the king's house.

l: attempted sale of Ulysses into slavery, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: A Phoenician persuades the disguised Ulysses to leave Egypt and later places him on a ship under the pretense of carrying cargo to Libya. The ship's crew then intends to sell him as a slave, but he escapes by sliding down the rudder and swimming ashore near Ithaca.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Eumaeus says he does not believe the stranger's claim that Ulysses will return soon. The disguised Ulysses proposes that, if his master comes home, Eumaeus should give him good clothing and send him to Dulichium.

l: supper at Eumaeus’s hut, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Eumaeus and the swineherds prepare and share a sacrificial supper with the disguised Ulysses. Eumaeus gives Ulysses specially honored slices from the loin, and Mesaulius supplies bread.

l: hospitality, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: Eumaeus offers hospitality to the disguised Ulysses even though he doubts his story. He explains that he does so from respect for Jove, the god of hospitality, and pity for a stranger in distress.

l: warfare, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The disguised Ulysses says that he was naturally inclined toward ships, fighting, javelins, and arrows rather than farming or domestic life. He claims to have led ambushes, killed enemies, and commanded foreign campaigns before Troy.

l: hardship and misfortune, The Odyssey, “I am by birth a Cretan; my father was a well to do man, who had many
s: The disguised Ulysses recounts repeated hardship, including poverty after his father's death, defeat in Egypt, years in Egypt and Phoenicia, attempted enslavement, shipwreck, drifting at sea, and arrival in Ithaca wearing rags. Eumaeus responds with pity despite refusing to believe the account of Ulysses's return.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Minerva tells Telemachus to leave Lacedaemon, return to Ithaca, avoid the suitors’ ambush, and go first to Eumaeus’s hut. Telemachus receives valuable gifts from Menelaus and Helen, travels with Pisistratus to Pylos, and then boards his ship. At Pylos he accepts the exiled seer Theoclymenus as a suppliant and brings him aboard. The ship sails toward Ithaca with a favorable wind, while Telemachus wonders whether he will escape capture or death.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Minerva goes to Lacedaemon and tells Telemachus to return home at once. She warns him that the suitors are lying in wait for him and instructs him to send his ship to Ithaca while he goes to Eumaeus.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Telemachus leaves Lacedaemon after receiving gifts from Menelaus and Helen. He travels with Pisistratus to Pylos, boards his ship, accepts Theoclymenus as a suppliant, and sails toward Ithaca.

l: Pisistratus, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Pisistratus helps Telemachus prepare to leave Lacedaemon and drives him to Pylos. At Telemachus’s request, he leaves him at the ship and returns to tell his father, Nestor, what has happened.

l: Menelaus, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Menelaus agrees to let Telemachus return home and gives him a silver-and-gold mixing bowl. He also provides hospitality, sends him off with a drink-offering, and asks him to tell Nestor how kindly he treated them.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Ulysses is described as having been away for a long time, and Telemachus is searching for news of him. Helen interprets the eagle carrying a goose as an omen that Ulysses will return and take revenge on the suitors, if he has not already returned.

l: Penelope, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Penelope remains in Ithaca while Telemachus is away. Minerva says that her father and brothers are urging her to marry Eurymachus, who has given her more wedding presents than the other suitors.

l: Theoclymenus, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Theoclymenus, an exiled seer from Argos, approaches Telemachus at Pylos and asks for protection after killing a man of his own race. Telemachus accepts him as a suppliant and brings him aboard the ship.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: The suitors are consuming Telemachus’s property in Ithaca. Their chief men lie in wait in the Strait between Ithaca and Samos, intending to kill him before he reaches home.

l: Telemachus's crew, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Telemachus’s crew prepares the ship, boards it, and follows his orders. The men set up the mast, raise the sails, and sail with him and Theoclymenus toward Ithaca.

l: Lacedaemon, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Lacedaemon is where Telemachus and Pisistratus are staying at Menelaus’s house. Telemachus leaves it after Minerva urges him to return home.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Ithaca is Telemachus’s home, where Penelope and the suitors remain. Minerva directs Telemachus to return there, and the ship eventually heads toward it.

l: Pylos, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Pylos is where Telemachus parts from Pisistratus and boards his ship. It is also where Theoclymenus finds him and joins the voyage.

l: the ship, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Telemachus’s ship waits at Pylos with the crew and Menelaus’s gifts aboard. Minerva sends a strong favorable wind, and the ship sails past Crouni and Chalcis toward Pheae, Elis, and the flying islands.

l: Telemachus's return from Pylos, The Odyssey, BOOK XV
s: Minerva urges Telemachus to return home quickly because the suitors threaten him and Penelope may be forced to marry Eurymachus. Telemachus leaves Lacedaemon, reaches Pylos, and begins the sea journey toward Ithaca, uncertain whether he will escape capture or death.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Ulysses tests Eumaeus by proposing to beg in the city, but Eumaeus urges him to remain at the hut until Telemachus returns. Eumaeus recounts how he was carried from Syra by Phoenicians and sold to Laertes. Meanwhile, Telemachus reaches Ithaca, sends Theoclymenus to Piraeus for hospitality, and goes to the swineherd’s homestead. A hawk carrying a dove appears on Telemachus’s right, and Theoclymenus interprets it as an omen of Telemachus’s future power.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Ulysses tells Eumaeus that he wants to go to the city to beg and possibly visit Ulysses’ house and the suitors. He praises Eumaeus for treating him kindly, asks about Ulysses’ parents, and listens with pity to Eumaeus’s story.

l: Eumaeus, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Eumaeus is disturbed by Ulysses’ plan to approach the suitors and advises him to remain at the station until Telemachus returns. He recounts that he was born on Syra, was carried away by Phoenicians, and was sold to Laertes.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Telemachus reaches Ithaca with his crew and sends the ship toward the city while he goes to inspect the herdsmen on one of his farms. He entrusts Theoclymenus to Piraeus and then walks to the homestead where Eumaeus keeps the swine.

l: Penelope, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Ulysses says that he could bring Queen Penelope news of her husband if he went to Ulysses’ house. Telemachus says that she usually remains in an upper chamber at her loom and does not often show herself to the suitors.

l: Laertes, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Laertes is still living and prays to die peacefully in his own house. He is deeply distressed by Ulysses’ absence and by the death of his wife, and he once gave goods to obtain Eumaeus.

l: Theoclymenus, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Theoclymenus asks Telemachus where he should stay in Ithaca. After seeing a hawk carrying a dove, he interprets the sight as a sign that Telemachus will remain powerful and that no house in Ithaca will be more royal than his.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Ulysses considers begging among the suitors and says he could serve them in many ways. Eumaeus warns that their pride and insolence are extreme, while Telemachus calls Eurymachus the most persistent of the suitors courting Penelope.

l: Phoenicians, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Phoenician traders come to Syra in a ship loaded with merchandise. They persuade a Phoenician woman to help them escape with Eumaeus, sail away with him, and later sell him to Laertes.

l: Syra, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Syra is described as an island lying above Ortygia. It has good soil, pasture for cattle and sheep, wine and wheat, two communities, and inhabitants who are said to suffer neither famine nor sickness.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: The Phoenician ship carrying Eumaeus is driven to Ithaca, where Laertes obtains him. Telemachus returns to Ithaca and travels toward the city and the homestead of the swineherd.

l: the swineherd's hut, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Ulysses and Eumaeus eat and drink in the swineherd’s hut with the other men. They remain there talking about their hardships until nearly daybreak.

l: town, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Ulysses proposes going around the city to beg for drink and bread and to visit Ulysses’ house and the suitors. Telemachus tells the crew to take the ship on to the city while he goes to the herdsmen.

l: Phoenician ship, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: The Phoenician ship stays at Syra for a year while its traders load precious merchandise. It carries away the Phoenician woman and Eumaeus, sails for six days and nights, and is then taken by winds and waves to Ithaca.

l: begging and hunger, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Ulysses proposes to begin begging in the town so that he will not trouble Eumaeus or his men. He plans to ask for drink and bread and to offer his services to the suitors.

l: hospitality, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Eumaeus provides food and drink for respectable strangers who come to his station. Telemachus entrusts Theoclymenus to Piraeus, who promises that the stranger will lack nothing in hospitality.

l: hawk omen, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: A hawk carrying a dove in its talons flies on Telemachus’s right, and feathers fall between him and the ship. Theoclymenus identifies it as a divine omen of Telemachus’s continuing power and royal status in Ithaca.

l: Phoenician abduction of Eumaeus, The Odyssey, Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the
s: Eumaeus says that Phoenicians took him from Syra after a Phoenician woman led him out of his father’s house. The traders carried him away by ship and sold him to Laertes, who gave goods in exchange for him.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Telemachus returns from Pylos to the swineherd's station, where he meets Ulysses in disguise. Minerva transforms Ulysses into a youthful form, and he reveals himself to Telemachus as his father. Father and son make plans to destroy the suitors, conceal Ulysses's identity, and remove the household's arms. Eumaeus is sent to tell Penelope that Telemachus has returned, while Ulysses and Telemachus prepare to go to the city.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Ulysses stays at the swineherd's station disguised as a Cretan beggar. With Minerva's help, he resumes a youthful and imposing appearance, reveals himself to Telemachus, and begins planning the destruction of the suitors.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Telemachus returns safely from Pylos and comes to the swineherd's station. After learning that Ulysses is his father, he embraces him, discusses the suitors' numbers, and agrees to help prepare for their destruction.

l: Eumaeus, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Eumaeus joyfully welcomes Telemachus at the station and provides food and a place to sit. At Telemachus's instruction, he goes secretly to tell Penelope that Telemachus has returned.

l: Penelope, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Penelope remains in Ulysses's house, grieving and weeping continually. She has not rejected the suitors outright or concluded the matter of remarriage, and Telemachus orders that she be told secretly of his return.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Minerva appears to Ulysses in the form of a woman and tells him that the time has come to reveal himself to Telemachus. She transforms Ulysses into a younger, better-clothed man and urges him to plan the destruction of the suitors.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: The suitors consume Telemachus's estate while pretending to court Penelope. They are numerous and insolent, and Ulysses and Telemachus plan to destroy them.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Ithaca is the country to which Ulysses has returned after a twenty-year absence. Its principal men, along with chiefs from neighboring islands, participate in consuming Ulysses's household under the pretext of courting Penelope.

l: the swineherd's station, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: The swineherd's station shelters Ulysses in disguise and receives Telemachus after his return from Pylos. It is the place where Minerva enables Ulysses to reveal himself and where father and son first make their plans.

l: house of Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Ulysses's house is controlled by the suitors, who waste its provisions and mistreat its household. Telemachus and Ulysses plan to return there and remove its arms before confronting the suitors.

l: the armour, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Ulysses orders Telemachus to collect the arms in the house and hide them in the strong store room. Telemachus is to explain that they are being moved because smoke has damaged them and because arms might encourage quarrels during the suitors' drinking.

l: Telemachus's return from Pylos, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Telemachus returns safely from Pylos and goes directly to the swineherd's station. He asks Eumaeus about Penelope and later sends Eumaeus to announce his return to her.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Ulysses has reached Ithaca after a long wandering and much hardship, transported by the Phaeacians while he slept. Their gifts to him remain hidden in a cave.

l: Ulysses's revelation to Telemachus, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Minerva directs Ulysses to stop concealing his identity from Telemachus. Ulysses reveals that he is Telemachus's father, and the two embrace and weep before discussing how to deal with the suitors.

l: the suitors’ abuse of Telemachus’s household, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: The suitors waste Ulysses's bread and wine, consume his estate, and behave insolently in his house. They also mistreat strangers and drag the women servants about the house in an unseemly way.

l: the suitors’ courtship of Penelope, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: The suitors from Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, and Ithaca court Penelope while refusing to leave Ulysses's household. Penelope neither openly rejects them nor brings the matter to a conclusion.

l: revenge upon the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XVI
s: Ulysses and Telemachus plan to return to the house, conceal Ulysses's identity, remove most of the arms, and confront the suitors with help from Minerva and Jove. Telemachus will appear to act normally among the suitors while Ulysses returns disguised as a beggar.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Telemachus returns from his voyage to Pylos, while his ship reaches Ithaca and is drawn into the harbour. The suitors learn that he has escaped their ambush and discuss killing him, but Amphinomus urges them to seek the gods' guidance. Penelope, informed of the plot by Medon, rebukes Antinous and the suitors for consuming Ulysses's property and seeking her marriage. At the countryside house, Eumaeus reports the ship's arrival to Telemachus and Ulysses, while Minerva disguises Ulysses so that Eumaeus will not recognize him.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Telemachus returns safely from Pylos, though he goes into the country rather than immediately returning to the house. He sends his ship to Ithaca to prevent Penelope from becoming alarmed, and later learns from Eumaeus that a ship carrying armed men has entered the harbour.

l: Eumaeus, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Eumaeus privately tells Penelope that Telemachus has returned and then goes back to his pigs. He later reports to Telemachus and Ulysses that he saw an armed ship enter the harbour, without knowing for certain that it belonged to the suitors.

l: Penelope, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Penelope learns of the suitors' plot against Telemachus from Medon. She appears before the suitors, rebukes Antinous for plotting against her son and consuming Ulysses's property, and then goes upstairs to mourn Ulysses until Minerva puts her to sleep.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Ulysses remains with Telemachus and Eumaeus at the countryside house. Minerva changes him into an old man and restores his old clothing so that Eumaeus will not recognize him and reveal his identity to Penelope.

l: Antinous, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Antinous urges the suitors to kill Telemachus before he can address the Achaeans in assembly. He proposes seizing Telemachus on his farm or on the road and dividing Ulysses's property among the suitors, while sending Penelope and the man who marries her to the house.

l: Eurymachus, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Eurymachus first proposes sending a ship after Telemachus, before learning that Telemachus's ship has already returned. He falsely reassures Penelope that Telemachus has nothing to fear from the suitors while secretly plotting against him.

l: Amphinomus, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Amphinomus notices that Telemachus's ship has entered the harbour and tells the suitors that they need not send a message. He opposes killing Telemachus without first consulting the gods, though he says he will help if the oracles of Jove approve.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: The suitors are surprised and angry when Telemachus returns safely. They gather in council, discuss killing him, and return to the house of Ulysses, where Penelope confronts them over their plot and their consumption of Ulysses's property.

l: immortal gods, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: The suitors believe that a god helped Telemachus escape their watch and return home. Amphinomus proposes that they consult the gods before deciding whether to kill him, and Minerva later disguises Ulysses and puts Penelope to sleep.

l: Pylos, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Pylos is the place from which Telemachus and his crew return. Eumaeus tells Penelope that Telemachus has come back from Pylos.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Ithaca is where Telemachus's ship arrives and where the suitors gather after returning from their failed attempt to intercept him. The suitors fear that the people of Ithaca will oppose them if their plot becomes known.

l: the house of Ulysses, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: The house of Ulysses receives the returning suitors, who take their accustomed seats there. Penelope comes into its court to confront them, while Telemachus and Ulysses prepare and eat supper at a separate countryside house.

l: the ship, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Telemachus's ship reaches Ithaca, is drawn onto the land, and has its armour and presents removed. A servant is sent to tell Penelope that the ship has returned while Telemachus remains in the country.

l: the estate of Ulysses, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: The suitors plan to divide Ulysses's property among themselves if they kill Telemachus. Penelope condemns them for devouring it without paying and for attempting to take Ulysses's wife and kill his son.

l: marriage to Penelope, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Antinous proposes that, if Telemachus is killed, Penelope and the man who marries her should receive the house. He also suggests that, if Telemachus is allowed to live, the suitors should make separate offers to Penelope and let her marry the man who offers the most.

l: the suitors' plot to kill Telemachus, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: The plot fails because Telemachus returns before the suitors can capture him. The suitors then consider killing him at his farm or on the road, while Penelope learns of their plan from Medon and publicly rebukes Antinous.

l: Telemachus's journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon, The Odyssey, Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought
s: Telemachus's voyage to Pylos ends with his safe return. His ship reaches Ithaca before the suitors can intercept it, and he sends the ship onward while he goes into the country.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Telemachus returns home from his journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon, reunites with Penelope, and tells her that Menelaus learned Ulysses is alive but held by Calypso. Theoclymenus declares that Ulysses is already in Ithaca, investigating the suitors’ crimes and preparing revenge. Ulysses and Eumaeus travel toward the city, where Melanthius insults Ulysses and kicks him. Ulysses endures the abuse and prepares to enter his own house as a beggar.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Telemachus returns to his house and embraces Penelope, then tells her about his journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon. He asks her to prepare offerings to the gods and goes to the assembly before joining Theoclymenus at home.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Ulysses remains disguised as an old beggar and travels from the swineherd’s station toward the city with Eumaeus. Melanthius insults and kicks him, but Ulysses controls his anger and endures the abuse.

l: Eumaeus, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Eumaeus obeys Telemachus by taking Ulysses toward the city, giving him a stick for the rough road. He rebukes Melanthius for insulting Ulysses and advises Ulysses about entering the house.

l: Penelope, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Penelope joyfully welcomes Telemachus home but continues to grieve for Ulysses. She hears Telemachus’s report that Ulysses is being held by Calypso and listens to Theoclymenus’s assurance that Ulysses is in Ithaca.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: The suitors greet Telemachus with outward friendliness and inward malice, while he avoids them. They continue their insolent behavior, engaging in contests and preparing a lavish meal.

l: Melanthius, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Melanthius meets Eumaeus and Ulysses on the road and verbally abuses Ulysses, predicting that stools will be thrown at him if he approaches Ulysses’s house. He kicks Ulysses and later joins the suitors inside.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Ithaca is the homeland to which Telemachus returns and toward which Ulysses travels in disguise. Theoclymenus declares that Ulysses is already in Ithaca, either moving through the countryside or staying in one place.

l: town of Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: The city is the destination to which Telemachus returns and where Ulysses is expected to beg. Eumaeus and Ulysses approach it by way of a fountain surrounded by poplars and an altar to the nymphs.

l: house of Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Ulysses observes that his house is large and well-built, with successive buildings, battlemented walls, and strong double doors. The house is filled with people feasting and music as Ulysses approaches it disguised as a beggar.

l: the suitors' feast, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: The suitors sacrifice sheep, goats, pigs, and a heifer before preparing their meal. Their feast is accompanied by music, and servants bring them portions of meat and bread.

l: Telemachus's journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Telemachus reports that Nestor welcomed him at Pylos but knew nothing about Ulysses. In Lacedaemon, Menelaus told him that the old man of the sea had seen Ulysses on an island, grieving in Calypso’s house and unable to return.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Menelaus’s report says that Ulysses is alive but detained by Calypso because he lacks ships and sailors. Theoclymenus instead declares that Ulysses is already in Ithaca and preparing to reckon with the suitors.

l: revenge upon the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Telemachus asks Penelope to promise offerings to the gods if they grant revenge upon the suitors. Theoclymenus says that Ulysses is investigating the suitors’ wrongdoing and preparing a day of reckoning.

l: begging and hunger, The Odyssey, BOOK XVII
s: Telemachus sends Ulysses to the city to beg for drink and bread, since he cannot care for another burden. Ulysses says that hunger cannot be hidden and calls the cravings of the belly an enemy that troubles all people.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, As they were thus talking, a dog that had been lying asleep raised his
s: Ulysses, disguised as a poor beggar, enters the house and is recognized by his old dog Argos, who dies after recognizing him. Telemachus gives Ulysses food, while Antinous insults him and strikes him with a footstool. Penelope hears of the assault and sends for the stranger so she can question him about Ulysses, but he asks to wait until sundown. Eumaeus returns to the pigs, while Telemachus remains among the suitors and the suitors continue their singing and dancing.
